ap_calculus_bc-m01.stem: The graph of a decreasing positive function $f$ on $[1,8]$ is shown and consists of line segments, and $b_n=f(n)$. The alternating series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(-1)^{n+1}b_n$ is approximated by its partial sum $S_5$ of the first $5$ terms. Using the alternating series error bound, what is the least upper bound for $|S-S_5|$ that the graph supports, if $b_n$ continues to decrease to $0$ beyond $n=8$?

stimulus.description: Graph of f, consisting of line segments connecting the plotted vertices.

options.why: Uses the last term included in the partial sum, b_5, as the bound.
Reports the partial sum S_5 itself.
Uses the difference b_5 - b_6 of consecutive terms.
The error is at most the first omitted term b_6 = f(6), read from the graph.

blueprint.subject: ap_calculus_bc
blueprint.concept: Bound an alternating series error using terms read from a graph of the terms' function
student_thinking: Identify the first omitted term b_(N+1)

key_conditions.condition: terms are positive, decreasing and tend to 0, so the alternating series error bound applies

verification.independent_path: exact rational recomputation of the terms at integers and of the partial sum (independent of option construction)

ap_calculus_bc-m02.stem: A function $f$ has derivatives of all orders. The graph of its third derivative $f'''$ on $0\le x\le 3$ is shown and consists of line segments. The second-degree Maclaurin polynomial $P_2$ is used to estimate $f(0.9)$. What bound on $|f(0.9)-P_2(0.9)|$ does the Lagrange error bound give?

stimulus.description: Graph of the third derivative of f, consisting of line segments connecting the plotted vertices.

options.why: Uses the maximum of |f'''| over the whole graph instead of over [0, 0.9].
Error <= M |x|^3/3! where M is the maximum of |f'''| on [0, a] read from the graph; evaluate with a calculator.
Uses the value of f''' at x = 0.9 instead of its maximum absolute value.

blueprint.subject: ap_calculus_bc
blueprint.concept: Apply the Lagrange error bound for a second-degree polynomial with a bound on the third derivative read from a graph
student_thinking: Read the largest absolute value of f''' on [0, a] from the graph

key_conditions.condition: |f'''| <= M on [0, a] holds for the maximum absolute value on the interval
key_conditions.evidence: the graph is piecewise linear so the maximum occurs at a vertex or at x = a

misconceptions.description: uses the maximum from the whole graph

verification.independent_path: maximum absolute value from a 2000-point grid on [0, a] (independent of vertex reading)

ap_calculus_bc-m03.stem: A particle moves in the $xy$-plane. The graphs of $x'(t)$ and $y'(t)$ for $0\le t\le 8$ are shown and each consists of line segments. What is the total distance the particle travels from $t=0$ to $t=4$?

stimulus.description: Graphs of x'(t) and y'(t), each consisting of line segments connecting the plotted vertices.

options.why: Reports the length of the displacement vector, the straight-line distance between the start and end.
Integrates |x'| + |y'| instead of the speed sqrt((x')^2 + (y')^2).
Distance = integral of sqrt((x')^2 + (y')^2) from 0 to 4; the components come from the graphs and the integral is evaluated numerically with a calculator.
Uses the trapezoidal rule with only the vertex speeds, which is not the arc length for a speed that is curved between vertices.

blueprint.subject: ap_calculus_bc
blueprint.concept: Find the arc length of a parametric path from graphs of the velocity components using a calculator
student_thinking: Write the arc length integral of the speed sqrt((x')^2 + (y')^2)
Express x' and y' piece by piece from the graphs
Evaluate the integral numerically with a calculator

key_conditions.condition: distance traveled equals the integral of speed
key_conditions.evidence: arc length formula for parametric curves

verification.independent_path: composite Simpson rule on each segment of the speed function (independent of scipy quad)
